executive_summary: EUR/JPY closed at 177.63 on 2026-10-02, one session after the valuation date. It is down 1.94% over one month, 3.99% over three months and 4.51% over six months, but up 0.85% over twelve. Spot sits at the 18th percentile of its 52-week closing range (175.42–187.59), below a bearishly stacked set of daily moving averages: 50-day 182.19, 100-day 183.71, 200-day 183.99. The dominant bilateral story is policy convergence. The BoJ hiked to 1.25% on 2026-09-18 and its Summary of Opinions reads hawkish, while the ECB, at 2.50%, describes its own stance as a "measured response" against a curve that still prices about 70bp more. That has cut the policy gap to 125bp and set up two back-to-back meeting pairs (2026-10-29/30 and 2026-12-17/18) where the BoJ speaks last both times. The bilateral read differs from both single-currency dossiers. The euro dossier's Bearish score (-0.2651) comes mostly from dollar factors that fall away in a yen cross. The yen dossier's tactical liability, a crowded +72.0K speculative long, becomes a contrarian support for this pair. The settled verdict is Neutral tactically (conviction 2, score -0.0792) and Bearish strategically (conviction 3, score -0.3338). Our strategic base case is 172.80 by end-Q1 2027, against a derived six-month forward of 176.32, an edge of about 350 pips. Three caveats apply. Long EUR/JPY carry of about 125–147bp costs a short roughly 65 pips a quarter. The pair sits about 220–290 pips above a 52-week-low and Fibonacci cluster at 174.77–175.41. And roughly 4% of convergence is already in the price, even though the policy gap has narrowed only 25bp.

Carry is not the binding driver of this pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The policy gap is 125bp: ECB deposit rate 2.50% against BoJ 1.25%. It narrowed from 150bp when the BoJ's 7-2 hike took effect on 2026-09-24. The two-year gap tells the same story: the Schatz at 3.20% against the JGB 2y at 1.93% (both 2026-09-30) is 127bp, almost exactly the policy gap. Each curve prices roughly 70bp of further tightening over two years, so the market expects the differential to stay flat. Over the past month the repricing has gone against the euro leg. The chance of an ECB hike on 2026-10-29 fell from about 50% to under 30% after Lagarde called the policy a measured response. Meanwhile the BoJ delivered its hike, and its Summary of Opinions showed a hawkish majority. The tactical window ends on two back-to-back decisions: the ECB on 2026-10-29 (no projections) and the BoJ Outlook Report on 2026-10-30, so the BoJ speaks last. The policy channel transmits through the 2y spread. If both banks hold, the level of the gap is unchanged. The risk is lopsided, though: a BoJ hike priced at only 25-38% is more plausible than an ECB hike priced under 30% that the ECB's own guidance does not support. Confidence is low because the level has not moved and the deciding events fall at the very end of the window.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, delivery against pricing decides this factor, and the two dossiers expect opposite errors. The base dossier expects one more ECB hike, most likely on 2026-12-17 with projections, against about 2.8 hikes in the curve. It also argues that French spreads at 111.2bp cap the ECB's terminal rate. The quote dossier expects two BoJ hikes to 1.75% across 2026-10-30, 2026-12-18 and the 2027-01-22 Outlook Report, against a curve pricing roughly two hikes over twelve months. If the ECB adds 25bp and the BoJ adds 50bp, the policy gap falls from 125bp to 100bp, against a market that prices it flat. On top of that, the ECB's under-delivery against its own curve would cheapen the front end of the euro leg. The long end makes the same point: a Japanese investor hedging Bunds at roughly the 147bp futures-implied cost earns about 2.11%, against 3.06% on a 10y JGB. The Bund-JGB 10y pickup is only about 52bp even unhedged. The transmission is gradual erosion of euro demand from Japanese real money, plus a front-end spread that compresses at each meeting pair. The risks to this view are a BoJ stalled by the Takaichi administration, or euro core inflation climbing toward 2.8% and forcing the ECB to deliver what is priced.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The near-term data favour the euro leg. The euro area is growing 1.2% y/y and 0.6% q/q, against Japan at 0.73% y/y and 0.4% q/q, where private consumption contributed zero and capex fell 0.9%. Surprises point the same way. The euro-area September flash composite PMI beat at 53.1 against 51.7 expected. In Japan, the Tankan's large-manufacturer index missed at +24 against +25, August industrial production fell 1.7% against a forecast 1.4% rise, and household spending fell 3.6% y/y. Inflation leaves the ECB with more cover: euro headline 3.2% and core 2.4%, against Japanese headline 1.9% and core 1.7%, the seventh month below target. National September prints put the 2026-10-02 euro flash on a 3.8% track (a forecast, not a print). The mechanism is relative: firm euro data keep the December ECB hike live, while soft Japanese core data strengthen the Asada and Sato dissent against back-to-back BoJ moves. The caveat is that euro core is falling and wages are slowing to 3.0%, so the support is real but shallow.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the two economies swap advantages. On growth the euro area stays ahead: ECB projections put 2026 GDP at 0.9% and 2027 at 1.4%, while Japan's potential sits near 0.5-1% with consumption stagnant. On inflation persistence, though, the momentum is moving toward Japan. Euro core is falling to 2.4% and negotiated wages have slowed to 3.0%, and Lagarde says wages show no material response to the energy shock. Japan has a fourth straight Shunto above 5% at 5.01%, Tankan three-year inflation expectations at 2.6%, a 7.6% PPI, and energy subsidies whose roll-off will mechanically lift its headline. Both economies are energy importers paying a terms-of-trade tax, so the real-income drag hits both legs. In net terms, euro growth outperformance is offset by an inflation trajectory that strengthens the BoJ's case relative to the ECB's, and neither dominates.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the factor becomes an asymmetry argument. Credit at 83bp IG and VIX at 16 have far more room to widen than to tighten, and the yen has the highest G10 beta to that widening. Japan's roughly USD 3.5tn of foreign securities is fuel for repatriation in stress. The euro gains nothing from a risk-off episode and, as a non-haven energy importer, loses. Carry-unwind fuel is smaller than in past cycles: JPY speculators are already net long, and estimates of total yen carry run to USD 300-500bn rather than the larger 2024 book. That reduces the size of a move but not its direction. Iran tails cut both ways for this pair, because a Hormuz settlement helps both importers and a re-escalation hurts both. In risk-off, though, the FX haven channel has historically dominated the trade channel for the yen over one to three months.

strategic.contrarian_case: The case against the bearish structural read is that the yen carry trade has rebuilt itself many times on similar setups. If the BoJ stalls at 1.25% under political pressure, a 125bp positive carry with low cross volatility could draw systematic euro buyers back. The euro is also the second-largest reserve currency, with a slow, price-insensitive diversification bid.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both economies are large energy importers whose external accounts are deteriorating on energy, so the factor largely nets out. The euro area ran a July goods surplus of EUR 14.2bn, but within it an energy deficit of EUR 28.0bn, with energy imports up 13.9% y/y. Its current account fell to EUR 27.6bn from EUR 35.1bn (1.92% of GDP on the Q1 vintage). Japan's August goods balance was -1,105.6bn yen, the fourth straight deficit, with crude imports up 58.7%. Its 5.03%-of-GDP current account rests on primary income that is largely reinvested abroad rather than converted into yen. Direct bilateral trade is too small to move the pair: IMF DOTS shows EUR exports to Japan of USD 63.7bn against imports of USD 60.1bn in 2024, a euro surplus of USD 3.6bn. Japan's mirror data show a wider gap (USD 67.9bn imports from the EU against USD 55.5bn exports). Over four weeks, the monthly trade settlements on each side are both mild sellers of their own currency, and they offset.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, each leg's specific energy vulnerability decides the factor, and the two offset. Japan is more exposed to crude: it imports about 99% of its oil, 94.2% of its crude from the Middle East, and the dossiers show Brent between 98.48 and 114.89 dollars (see assumptions), up about 54% y/y. The euro area is more exposed to gas into winter: EU storage is about 70%, some 12 points below a year earlier, and TTF is EUR 72.90/MWh against the ECB's EUR 51.0 assumption. Japan is not insulated from gas either, since Asian LNG spot prices rose more than 140% after the Ras Laffan strike. Under the framework's netting rules, oil up is double-negative for JPY and single-negative for EUR, which supports the pair. TTF up is negative for EUR, which pressures the pair. LNG up is double-negative for JPY, which supports the pair. A cold winter therefore hits both. The commodity sensitivities net to a mild pair-positive tilt from oil, offset by Europe's worse winter gas buffer, leaving no edge either way.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices the energy premium draining in both regions. A winter gas shock would hurt the euro relatively more, and an oil shock would hurt the yen relatively more. These two risks roughly offset, so this factor offers no relative edge on the pair.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral on both horizons. Both legs pay a terms-of-trade bill of similar sign. Japan's is oil-weighted and Europe's is gas-weighted into winter, so the strategic weight of 0.16 contributes nothing to the net score rather than tipping it.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: EUR: large net energy importer. Gas (TTF) is the dominant sensitivity heading into winter with storage at about 70%; oil is a secondary negative. EU energy imports EUR 41.3bn in July, +13.9% y/y.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: JPY: near-total oil importer (about 99%, 94.2% of crude from the Middle East) and large LNG importer. Crude is the dominant sensitivity; crude imports were 1.191tn yen in August, +58.7% y/y.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Oil: EUR negative (single), JPY negative (double). Netting gives the yen leg the larger loss, so oil up means pair up and oil down means pair down. Gas/TTF: EUR negative with no direct JPY rule, so TTF up means pair down. LNG/JKM: JPY double-negative, so JKM up means pair up. TTF and JKM usually move together in a global LNG shock, so a broad gas spike is close to neutral for the pair, while a Europe-specific gas squeeze (storage-driven) is pair-negative. The net result is a modest positive oil beta for EUR/JPY, offset by Europe's specific winter storage vulnerability.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Mildly pair-positive. Japan's goods deficit widens faster than the euro area's energy bill, which favours the euro against the yen at the margin, unless the move comes from a Hormuz re-escalation that also triggers a yen haven bid (Factor 3).
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Mildly pair-negative. It relieves Japan's crude-heavy import bill more than the euro area's gas-heavy one. A settlement-driven fall would also ease TTF, partly offsetting the effect.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Brent crude through the JPY leg, with Dutch TTF through the EUR leg as the winter counterweight. The Strait of Hormuz is the common node that moves both.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: For each bank, guidance and pricing diverge, and the two gaps point opposite ways. The ECB's 10 September statement refuses to pre-commit. Lagarde calls the hike a measured response on a middle path and says the Bank does not react to energy prices as such. Schnabel, the leading hawk, says policy can tolerate a more gradual return to target. Yet the curve carries about 70bp of further tightening, so the market is more hawkish than the ECB. The BoJ is the reverse: it says it will continue to raise the policy rate, and the 2026-09-30 Summary of Opinions shows a majority favouring further hikes and one member arguing for a faster pace, while OIS prices the October move at only 25-38%. The BoJ is more hawkish than its market. Sequencing amplifies this: the ECB speaks on 2026-10-29 and the BoJ answers with an Outlook Report on 2026-10-30. Credibility caveats apply to both banks: the BoJ has a history of opacity and faces political pressure from the Takaichi administration, and the BoJ vote was 7-2.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the opposing gaps compound across scheduled communication events. The BoJ has two Outlook Reports in or near the window (2026-10-30, 2027-01-22) plus 2026-12-18. Each is a vehicle to raise its inflation path, and it has now delivered two hikes in 2026 against political preference. The ECB's next projection round on 2026-12-17 must mark its EUR 51.0/MWh gas assumption to a market at EUR 72.90. That points to higher near-term inflation alongside weaker real incomes, a mix the Governing Council has already said it will answer only with measured steps. Schnabel's conditions (anchored expectations, demand resilience, the drag from global yields) read as a hawk's case for patience. The ECB's credibility is not the issue; its delivery against pricing is. The BoJ's credibility is improving from a low base, and the Ministry of Finance's coordinated intervention with the US Treasury adds a form of exchange-rate guidance that caps yen weakness. The main risk is political: a Takaichi administration that presses the BoJ to pause.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Event risk is asymmetric. The euro leg carries a dated, home-grown political risk; the yen leg carries a fiscal-political risk plus an official floor. France presented a EUR 54bn consolidation on 2026-10-01 ahead of a 2026-11-17 parliamentary vote, after three governments in fourteen months. The risk premium builds inside the window even though the vote falls after it. On the Japanese side, PM Takaichi's 2026-10-05 address on expansionary fiscal policy is a yen negative. That is partly offset by the coordinated late-July US-Japan intervention, about 8.45tn yen from Japan with the US Treasury involved. It truncates the yen-weakness tail on USD/JPY and spills into the crosses, because yen purchases are broad-based. Iran outcomes hit both energy importers and largely cancel for the pair. On balance the dated euro-specific risk, together with the official cap on yen weakness, tilts the factor mildly pair-negative.

Japan's tails are a snap election (the quote dossier estimates about 15%) and the December FY2027 budget, which belongs more to Factor 8. A second coordinated intervention (about 20%, conditional on USD/JPY revisiting the trigger zone) is a yen-positive tail with no euro-side equivalent. The largest common tail, Iran, is close to neutral for the pair under the commodity netting in Factor 5. Taken together, the event distribution is modestly skewed against the euro relative to the yen, but with wide dispersion.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Over four weeks the acute fiscal stress is on the euro side. The OAT-Bund spread is 111.2bp, the widest since 2012, against a one-year average of 74.2bp. French debt is 119.3% of GDP, Fitch rates France A+, and the ECB's Transmission Protection Instrument is not designed for fundamentals-driven widening, so there is no mechanical ceiling. Japan's debt is far larger at about 260% of GDP, but it has no near-term trigger. Ratings are stable at A1/A+/A, the late-September 40-year JGB auction drew the strongest demand since 2020, and JGB yields fell 2.5-4bp across the curve on 2026-09-30 on reports of fiscal reassurance from the Takaichi administration. Spreads transmit through euro risk premia: by the base dossier's correlation, each 10bp of OAT-Bund widening costs the euro broadly. Japan is not currently charging a comparable premium on the yen.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both sovereigns face dated fiscal tests, and the risks balance. The euro faces the 2026-11-17 French vote and a debt path toward 121.7% of GDP by 2027. That is partly offset by German fiscal expansion (2027 spending EUR 555.4bn, defence EUR 109.7bn), which supplies safe assets over a longer horizon. Japan faces the December FY2027 budget, which Fitch has said it will scrutinise. The 30y JGB is at 4.15% against a 1.93% 2y, a 222bp spread that increasingly reflects term premium rather than policy, and each 100bp on the average yield eventually costs about 2% of GDP in debt service. Higher JGB yields help the yen through the differential channel but hurt it through the sovereign-risk channel, and which dominates depends on the December budget. With France's acute risk set against Japan's larger but slower-moving stock problem, the factor nets to Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar conditions are tight in price but not in quantity, and they affect both legs of this cross similarly. The Fed hiked 12-0 to 3.75-4.00% on 2026-09-16, the dollar index gained about 2% in September, and the broad trade-weighted dollar index rose 1.88 to 120.33. Quantitative tightening ended in December 2025 and reserve-management purchases continue, so there is no funding stress. The estimated three-month cross-currency bases are similar for the two legs: about -17bp for EUR/USD and about -21bp for JPY/USD, both derived as residuals rather than quoted. So neither leg is materially cheaper to fund in dollars. The EUR/JPY futures roll of -147bp, against a 125bp policy gap, implies about 22bp of combined basis and term effects, which is unremarkable. On the dollar smile, the dollar sits on its exceptionalism side, which weighs on both legs. European banks' dollar borrowing and Japanese institutions' dollar hedging needs roughly offset.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.0792 falls inside the Neutral band (between -0.10 and +0.10), so the derived stance is Neutral, with a bearish tilt 0.021 short of the Bearish threshold. Four factors are Bearish (Policy, Guidance, Event Risk, Fiscal), two are Bullish (Inflation & Growth, contrarian Positioning) and four are Neutral. The two heaviest live factors largely cancel: Policy at -0.1296 against relative data momentum at +0.1044. The tilt is therefore carried by Guidance (-0.060) and the smaller euro-specific event and fiscal factors, offset by a crowded yen spec long (+0.054). This is breadth with little depth. No single factor has confidence above 60, and the deciding event, the BoJ Outlook Report on 2026-10-30, falls at the very end of the window.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the verdict is shaped by Policy & Rates (0.24) and Inflation & Growth (0.18), and they point in opposite directions. The policy gap is 125bp after the BoJ's move to 1.25% took effect on 2026-09-24. The 2y gap of 127bp shows both curves pricing about 70bp of further tightening, so the market expects the differential to stay flat. The month's repricing has run against the euro leg: the October ECB hike was priced out from about 50% to under 30%, while the BoJ delivered and signalled more. Against that, the relative data flow favours the euro: a 53.1 flash PMI beat and 1.2% y/y growth versus a Tankan miss, a 1.7% industrial production shortfall and 0.73% Japanese growth. Euro core at 2.4% also gives the ECB more cover than Japanese core at 1.7%. The two dossiers interact in a revealing way. The euro dossier is Bearish (-0.2651) mainly on dollar factors that largely drop out of a yen cross. The yen dossier is Neutral (-0.028) because its crowded positioning offsets an under-priced BoJ. Bilaterally, that positioning liability becomes a contrarian support for EUR/JPY (+0.054), while opposing guidance gaps for the two banks become the clearest pair-specific negative (-0.060). What is priced is a hold-hold outcome and a flat differential. Our edge is that the BoJ Outlook Report on 2026-10-30 is more likely than its 25-38% pricing to hawkishly surprise, one day after an ECB on 2026-10-29 that the market has already priced out. The French budget, presented on 2026-10-01 ahead of a 2026-11-17 vote, adds a euro-specific premium. The path of least resistance is two-sided until the meeting pair, then tilted lower if the BoJ uses the Outlook Report. Catalysts are the 2026-10-02 euro flash, the 2026-10-05 Takaichi address, the 2026-10-06 Japanese wage data, the 2026-10-29 ECB and the 2026-10-30 BoJ. Conviction is 2 rather than 1 because four independent channels lean the same way. It is not 3 because the score sits inside the Neutral band, the deciding event falls at the window's edge, and the crowded yen long could lift the pair first.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: On the dossiers' standalone tactical scores, the spread for EUR/JPY (-0.265 vs -0.028, about -0.24) ranks only fifth among euro-short crosses, behind EUR/USD, EUR/AUD, EUR/SGD and EUR/NOK, because the yen dossier is itself tactically neutral. Among yen crosses, tactical yen strength is better expressed against CHF or SEK, where the yen dossier ranks the yen ahead. Our bilateral tactical score of -0.079 confirms EUR/JPY is not a priority tactical short: it is a wait-for-the-meeting-pair cross.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.3338 is clearly in the Bearish band, so the derived stance is Bearish. Five factors are Bearish, none Bullish, and five Neutral. The depth is concentrated: Policy (-0.144) and Guidance (-0.093) supply 71% of the net, and they express one thesis, the ECB under-delivering against its curve while the BoJ delivers against its own. Risk asymmetry, Japanese real-money flows and euro event risk add breadth, but each is low-confidence. The largest strategic weight, External Balance at 0.16, contributes zero because both legs are energy importers. Read the score as one well-anchored mechanism reinforced at the edges, not five independent confirmations.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the verdict is decided by Policy & Rates (0.24) and Guidance & Credibility (0.15), and both are Bearish for the same reason. The two curves price matching tightening, about 70bp each over two years, which is why the 2y gap of 127bp sits on top of the 125bp policy gap. But the banks are guiding in opposite directions relative to their markets. The ECB calls its stance a measured middle path, does not pre-commit, and its leading hawk says policy can tolerate a slower return to target, against about 2.8 priced hikes. The BoJ says it will keep raising rates and its Summary of Opinions shows a hawkish majority, against roughly two hikes priced over twelve months. The base dossier expects one ECB hike, on 2026-12-17; the quote dossier expects two BoJ hikes by 2027-01-22. If both are right, the gap falls to about 100bp against a market pricing it flat. Here the dossiers reinforce each other rather than conflict: euro Bearish (-0.270) and yen Bullish (+0.250) meet in the same pair through the same channel. The bilateral factors add three things the standalone views miss. First, a Japanese investor hedging Bunds at about 147bp earns about 2.11%, against 3.06% on JGBs, a structural loss of euro demand. Second, the yen is a haven and the euro is not, which skews the risk distribution from tight credit spreads. Third, the euro's heavier dated political calendar, from the 2026-11-17 French vote into its 2027 election cycle. External Balance, the heaviest non-policy weight, nets to zero: Japan's oil exposure and Europe's winter gas exposure offset, and on oil alone the pair has a mild positive beta. The path of least resistance is lower, stepping at the paired decisions on 2026-12-17/18 and the 2027-01-22 Outlook Report. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because 71% of the score rests on one mechanism. Two risks could break it: political pressure from the Takaichi administration stalling the BoJ at 1.25%, or euro core inflation rising toward 2.8% and forcing the ECB to deliver what is priced. Positive carry of about 125-147bp also charges a short position roughly 56-65 pips a quarter. It is not 2 because the mechanism has dated, scheduled ways to be proved right or wrong at three meeting pairs.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: On the dossiers' standalone strategic scores, EUR/JPY's spread (-0.270 vs +0.250, about -0.52) is among the widest in the set. Its distinguishing feature is mechanism: EUR/JPY is the only cross in the set where the two banks' guidance-versus-pricing errors directly oppose each other at back-to-back meetings.

No cross was derived from the separate EUR/USD and USD/JPY forecasts in the dossiers, because a bank's pair view can differ from the product of its leg views.
